7.0.0.en: 1 Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit. 2 The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men: they all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net. 3 Both hands are earnest to do evil; the prince asketh, and the judge asketh for a reward; and the great man, he uttereth his mischievous desire: so they wrap it up. 4 The best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge: the day of thy watchmen and thy visitation cometh; now shall be their perplexity. 5 Trust ye not in a friend, put ye not confidence in a guide: keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom. 6 For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house. 7 Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me. 8 Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me. 9 I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him, until he plead my cause, and execute judgment for me: he will bring me forth to the light, and I shall behold his righteousness. 10 Then she that is mine enemy shall see it, and shame shall cover her which said unto me, "Where is the LORD thy God?" Mine eyes shall behold her: now shall she be trodden down as the mire of the streets.

7.0.1.en: In this lawsuit all of humanity is exposed; it cannot justify its ingratitude and unfaithfulness before God, who is faithful in His love for it, and so it declares the bitter truth. It has become like a vine without fruit, and a fig tree without a firstripe fruit. Hatred has run through the blood of men, so they carry hatred, each person against his brother, and the shedding of blood has crept in among them without cause, and enmity has arisen even between the members of one family.

7.0.2.en: Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage.

7.0.3.en: There is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit. [1]

7.0.4.en: A painful picture of the extent of the drought that has come upon the kingdom because of evil. This suits the age of Ahaz, the most wicked of the kings of Judah, or the beginning of the age of Hezekiah before the movement of reform. Some see that he is prophesying what the kingdom would come to in the days of Manasseh.

7.0.5.en: Judah and Jerusalem appear like an orchard after the gathering: the sight of the leaves is exceedingly beautiful, but a man cannot find a single cluster or a single fig to eat.

7.0.6.en: By saying, "Woe is me," he reckons that what has befallen the whole kingdom has befallen him alone, since he ascribes to himself every bitterness in which the people live, as though he himself tastes it. These are the true feelings of the men of God, and so we hear the groans of the prophet Jeremiah: "My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at my very heart; my heart maketh a noise in me" (Jer 4:19). "When I would comfort myself against sorrow, my heart is faint in me... For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt; I am black; astonishment hath taken hold on me" (Jer 8:18, 21).

7.0.7.en: * Who is speaking when the prophet says: "Woe is me, O my soul, for I have become as one who gathers stubble in the harvest"? Is the prophet gathering literal stubble, or even wanting to gather? Does the prophet have a field? In any case, the only One who truly gathers from what He has sown as a harvest is not the prophet but the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. And since there are many errors among the pagan nations, and also among those who are thought to belong to the Church, the prophet therefore grieves and laments over our sins when he says: "Woe is me, for I have become as one who gathers stubble" (Mic 7:1). Let each one examine himself carefully. Is he an ear of wheat? Does the Son of God discover in him something to pick up or to reap? Do we find some of us carried away by the winds? Even if we are still very few in ourselves, two or three grains, our sins are many against us. Looking at the churches, or those called churches, full of sinners, he says: "Woe is me, for I have come as one who gathers grass at the time of harvest, and as one who gathers the gleanings of the grapes at the time of making wine. (The Lord) comes seeking fruit from the vine, for each one of us has been planted as a vine in a fertile land (Isa 5:1), or as a vine brought out of Egypt (Ps 80:8), but it was planted to bear fruit (Jer 2:21). He comes to gather, and finds the gleanings of grapes, and a few clusters; it is neither flourishing nor fruitful. Who among us bears the clusters of virtue?"

7.0.8.en: Origen * The wicked are sifted like light chaff, but the righteous are saved like heavy wheat. Therefore take heed to the Lord when He says to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32). Those who are sifted like chaff perish, but he who does not perish, who is like the seed that falls and grows, increases and brings forth much fruit (Lk 8:8). Thus the prophet says: "Woe is me, for I have become as one who gathers the gleanings (the remains of the harvest) in the harvest." So evil is likened to gleanings, which are quickly burned with the dust. Therefore Job said: "They are as stubble before the wind" (Job 21:18). And immediately he added a short line, saying: "and as chaff that the storm carrieth away." Truly, so that he may know that the wicked is quickly crumbled and scattered like dust, you find this stated in the first Psalm: "like the dust which the wind driveth away from the face of the earth."

7.0.9.en: St. Ambrose The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men.

7.1.0.en: They all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net. [2]

7.1.1.en: The good man has perished from the earth, and no one upright is found any longer among men: the rulers seize possessions, the judges take bribes, treachery has crept in among friends, and hatred among the members of one family. Thus corruption has become general among the people. But God remains faithful, leading His people out of darkness into His marvelous light.

7.1.2.en: The human kingdom has turned into a forest in which each wants to devour the other; its law is injustice and the shedding of blood, and each person finds his happiness in hunting his brother as though with a net. As the Psalmist says: "Help, LORD; for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men. They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak" (Ps 12:1-2).

7.1.3.en: * Let us grieve for a while, that we may rejoice eternally. Let us fear the Lord; let us be the first to confess our sins to Him. Let us correct our apostasy and amend our errors, lest it be said of us: "Woe is me, O my soul, for the godly man is perished out of the earth, and there is none among men who mends their ways" (Mic 7:2) LXX.

7.1.4.en: St. Ambrose * I mean that if travel is in itself a hardship, it is even more so when the traveler is alone and there is no one to share his journey; this is the case here. In other words, fellowship and brotherly encouragement are no small matter. Therefore Paul also says: "And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works" (Heb 10:24). For this reason the ancients deserved to be adorned (spiritually), not because they practiced virtue, but because they practiced it despite its absence, with those who did it being rare in every place. This, in any case, is what Scripture means by saying: "Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations" (Gen 6:9).

7.1.5.en: On this basis we marvel at Abraham, at Lot, and at Moses, for they shone like stars in the midst of thick darkness, like roses among thorns, and like a flock among countless wolves, walking the way opposite to everyone else and without hesitation. You see how difficult the matter is in company when one takes a direction contrary to many; when he travels in the opposite direction to the crowd, he will suffer many troubles. Just as a ship finds it difficult to sail when the waves drive it in the opposite direction, so the matter is more difficult in the case of virtue.

7.1.6.en: * "Woe is me... the good man is perished out of the earth" (Mic 7:1-2). This is our part, to grieve; or rather, we need to say this every day. For since our prayers avail nothing, nor our counsel nor our warning, it remains for us to weep. So Christ did, after He had urged those in Jerusalem and they gained nothing, He wept over their plight. So also the prophets did, and so let us also do. From now on it is a time for grief, tears, and lamentation. It is fitting for us also to say: "Call for the mourning women, that they may come; and send for cunning women, that they may come" (Jer 9:17). Perhaps by this we can remove the sickness of those who surround themselves with lands that they acquire by plunder.

7.1.7.en: * Nothing is more troublesome and disturbing than gathering with a people such as this, for smoke and soot do not harm the eyes as fellowship with the wicked destroys souls.

7.1.8.en: St. John Chrysostom Both hands are earnest to do evil.

7.2.0.en: The prince and the judge ask for a reward, and the great man uttereth his mischievous desire: so they wrap it up. [3]

7.2.1.en: What the kingdom has reached is more hideous than a forest, for there is a studied plan: the leaders work together, but without the spirit of love, and their aim is plunder, robbery, and murder. The two hands of each of them are earnest in hunting souls and destroying them. What their hearts desire, and what their thoughts are steeped in, their hands carry out with all diligence.

7.2.2.en: The leaders, who were entrusted with defending the right, have used their authority to acquire wealth, so they ask for bribery in the form of gifts; thus they clothe vice in the garment of friendship and virtue.

7.2.3.en: By the great man is meant the man of wealth and authority, for he is not ashamed to speak frankly about the passion for the love of money in his soul, and so they corrupt their own souls as they corrupt the souls of those around them.

7.2.4.en: The best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge!

7.2.5.en: The day of thy watchmen and thy visitation cometh.

7.3.1.en: There is not one person who can be relied upon, for the best of them is sharp like a brier, and the wisest like a thorn hedge. Whoever approaches them receives from them nothing but wounds and troubles. They have become a desolate land, and the divine judgment has been pronounced against them: "Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field" (Gen 3:18), instead of being a holy heaven that yields the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, goodness, gentleness, and self-control (Gal 5:22-23).

7.3.2.en: Trust ye not in a friend.

7.3.3.en: Put ye not confidence in a guide.

7.4.0.en: Keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom. [5]

7.4.1.en: Among the things that grieved the heart of the prophet Micah is that, although they work together, a man does not trust his friend or his wife! Selfishness creeps in even among the members of the family, so each one works for himself and fears the other. Thus the family loses its social and spiritual warmth, and society dissolves through the spirit of selfishness and greed.

7.4.2.en: When deceit reigns over a man's life, he no longer trusts even her who is in his bosom. Abba Joseph sees that Samson, since he married a wicked, deceitful, and lying woman, was not able to carry out this commandment of the prophet Micah, and so he disclosed his secret after he had kept it for a long time, and that was the cause of great bitterness in his life.

7.4.3.en: Abba Isaac finds in this verse a call to secret prayer.

7.4.4.en: * Above all, we must observe with all care the commandment of the Gospel, which bids us enter into our closet, shut our door, and pray to our Father. This is fulfilled as follows:

7.4.5.en: * We pray within our closet when we remove from our inner hearts the disturbing thoughts and vain cares, and enter into a secret conversation, closed, between us and the Lord.

7.4.6.en: * We pray with the doors shut when we pray with closed lips, in quiet and complete silence, to Him who seeks hearts and not words.

7.4.7.en: * We pray in secret when we hide our petitions, which come from our hearts and our kindled minds, so that we disclose them to God alone, and the opposing powers (the demons) cannot discover them. Therefore we ought to pray in complete silence, not only to avoid disturbing our brethren next to us and troubling them with our whispering or loud words, and to avoid disturbing the thoughts of those praying with us, but also to hide the meaning of our petitions from our enemies who watch us, especially at the time of prayer, and thus the commandment is fulfilled: "Keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom" (Mic 7:5).

7.5.0.en: Abba Isaac For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house. [6]

7.5.1.en: Truly it is an evil time in which the son dishonors his father, the daughter rises up against her mother, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Thus even natural love is taken away from all.

7.5.2.en: The Lord Christ also referred to the attitude of unbelievers toward believers, even if they are their brothers or sons, saying: "And the brother shall deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child: and the children shall rise up against their parents, and cause them to be put to death. And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake" (Mt 10:21-22; Lk 21:16-17).

7.5.3.en: * What does the sword do? The sword of the Word cuts through defense. It practices the separation of the wicked from the good (Heb 4:12). In truth it creates a division between the believer and the unbeliever (Mt 10:35). It may even rouse the son, the daughter, and the bride against the father, the mother, and the mother-in-law, the active young against the imaginary elders.

7.5.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * "A man's foes shall be they of his own household" (Mt 10:36). For truly there is something like this among the Jews. That is, there are prophets and false prophets, so the people were divided against themselves, and there was dissension in families, some believing one and others the other. Therefore the prophet counsels them: "Trust ye not in a friend, put ye not confidence in a guide; keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom," and "a man's enemies are the men of his own house" (Mic 7:5-6).

7.5.5.en: St. John Chrysostom Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation.

7.6.1.en: General corruption does not justify our sliding into evil; if there is not one upright man among men, we must, with the prophet Micah, look to the Lord and await His salvation.

7.6.2.en: When a man confesses his evil and corruption, a door of hope opens in the surpassing work of God. For God, as a lover of mankind, in His anger is angry only at sin and cannot bear it, but as for the sinner, he is the object of His love. Therefore, by sincere repentance the Lord inclines His ears to hear his groaning and answers his cries.

7.6.3.en: When the prophet looked at the society around him, the matter seemed exceedingly grave, for it had become like a sick man whose recovery is not hoped for; but when he lifted the eyes of his heart to God, he saw the bright doors of hope before him, and his depths sang praise and glory to God, the giver of victory, who shines with His light upon the darkness and scatters it.

7.6.4.en: The prophet confesses that God has not changed; He who saved in the past saves now and will save, for He delighteth in mercy and does not retain His anger for ever.

7.6.5.en: * "Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the LORD his God" (Ps 146:5). Do you see the richness of the encouragement and counsel? Now when he points to blessedness, he means the receiving of all blessings, and he shows the horizons of hope. Therefore, after pointing to the blessedness of him who hopes in God, he showed the power of the Helper, indicating that the human being is different from God: the one perishes and the other remains. Not only does He remain, but His works remain too. Therefore he added: "Which made heaven, and earth, the sea, and all that therein is" (Ps 146:6)... and he adds, "Which keepeth truth for ever." This is His part; this is His habit; this is God's own mark; that He does not ignore those who err, nor neglect those in trial, but lifts up His hand for the victims of plotters, and does this continually.

7.6.6.en: St. John Chrysostom Thus when the picture grows very dark before the eyes of the men of God, they lift their gaze to God, hoping for His work, for He is the God of the impossible; there is no hope of salvation except in God alone, the Savior of the world. The prophet Micah did not hope in any man to set right the state of God's people, or of mankind, but looks to the Savior of the world alone. This is also what the Psalmist expressed in (Psalm 146).

7.6.7.en: * The prophet says to every person in general: do not rely on rulers, nor on emperors, nor governors, nor the judges of this world (see Ps 146:3)... Who are the rulers? Sons of men. Who are the sons of men? They are those in whom there is no salvation (Ps 146:3). "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth" (Ps 146:4). When he returns to his earth, what happens? "In that very day his thoughts perish." All reliance on rulers is vain; all their plans perish... Many rely on a ruler. He exists today; tomorrow he no longer exists.

7.6.8.en: St. Jerome By saying "I will wait for the God of my salvation," the prophet declares that he does not cast blame on the circumstances around him, nor on God who permitted the affliction, but accepts the discipline of the Lord with patience for the sake of his salvation and the salvation of his brethren. As Jeremiah the prophet says in his Lamentations: "Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins? Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD. Let us lift up our heart with our hands unto God in the heavens. We have transgressed and have rebelled" (Lam 3:39-42). Let us accuse ourselves and not accuse the days in which we live. Let us bear discipline as a motive for repentance, and so enjoy fellowship with "the God of our salvation"; then "my God will hear me."

7.6.9.en: Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy.

7.6.10.en: When I fall, I shall arise.

7.7.0.en: When I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me. [8]

7.7.1.en: When a man confesses his darkness and realizes that the Lord is a light to him, he no longer fears any enemy, as long as the Lord is with him. For though he fall and almost be broken, he finds God's hands lifting him up and raising him. As the Psalmist says: "Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand" (Ps 37:24). And if he sits in darkness, the Lord shines upon him and enlightens him. As he says: "That they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me" (Ps 86:17). So with every divine work in the life of the penitent, the enemy of good and his hosts are struck with disappointment, shame, and disgrace.

7.7.2.en: * Falling through weakness is not dangerous, if the man is free from the desire (to fall). Let it be your will to rise. He is ready, the One who raises you.

7.7.3.en: * Let us not rejoice at anyone's sin, but rather grieve, for it is written: "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me..." (Mic 7:8-10). And this is not without reason, for he who rejoices at another's fall rejoices at the victory of Satan. It is fitting for us to grieve when we hear of anyone perishing for whom Christ died. He does not despise even the stubble at the time of harvest... For it was said: "Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage" (see Mic 7:1), so that He may eat the firstfruits of the fruit of His grace in me.

7.7.4.en: St. Ambrose I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him, until he plead my cause, and execute judgment for me.

7.7.5.en: He will bring me forth to the light.

7.8.0.en: And I shall behold his righteousness. [9]

7.8.1.en: The coming of distress because of the spread of corruption drove the prophet to review himself and confess his fault against the Lord; therefore he accepts every discipline, and the Lord defends his uprightness. The person confesses his falls, and the Lord covers him with His righteousness and keeps him by His divine grace. The prophet does not see in the distress the Lord's rejection of him, but His divine desire to move him to repentance and to his enjoyment of fellowship with Him.

7.8.2.en: He feels his need for the hand of God working for his edification. This is the sign of receiving the divine light: complete surrender into the hands of God, the maker of good things and giver of righteousness.

7.8.3.en: * We sometimes bear a sickness as a punishment (discipline) for a sin, with the intention of changing us. Scripture says: "For whom the LORD loveth he correcteth" (Prov 3:12). Again Scripture teaches us: "For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep. For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:30-32). Therefore, when we who belong to this class recognize our transgressions, it becomes fitting to bear in silence, and without resorting to medicines, all the griefs that come upon us, remembering the words of the prophet: "I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him" (Mic 7:9). Moreover, we must show evidence of our change by showing fruits meet for repentance, remembering the words of the Lord: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (Jn 5:14). Sometimes also sickness comes upon us at the request of the evil one, and our Lord, the maker of good things, consents to condescend so that we enter into a battle with the evil one, reckoning him a mighty adversary, so that He nullifies his arrogance by the heroic patience of His servants.

7.8.4.en: St. Basil the Great Then she that is mine enemy shall see it, and shame shall cover her which said unto me:

7.9.0.en: Now shall she be trodden down as the mire of the streets. [10]

7.9.1.en: A wonderful picture of the life of victory! For when the believer enjoys the light of the Lord, he fears neither the darkness of the devil, nor the pleasure of sin, nor the weakness of the flesh, nor the deceit of the evil world. The enemy of good begins to taunt the one who has fallen, crying out in mockery: "Where is the LORD thy God?", as though God were unable to keep His children from falling. But when he sees the hand of God raising him up, shame strikes him.

7.9.2.en: In his fall, a man looks at himself and at the enemy's taunts against him, and sees himself like the mire of the streets under feet, to be trodden on; but when divine grace lifts him up, he realizes the possibilities of God working in him.

7.10.0.en: 11 In the day that thy walls are to be built, in that day shall the decree be far removed. 12 In that day also they shall come to thee from Assyria, and from the cities of Egypt, and from Egypt even to the river, and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain. 13 Notwithstanding the land shall be desolate because of them that dwell therein, for the fruit of their doings.

7.10.1.en: In the day that thy walls are to be built, in that day shall the decree be far removed. [11]

7.10.2.en: The believer enjoys an abundance of blessings, for he no longer fears the enemy with all his kingdom of darkness, being filled with hope that God Himself will be a divine wall protecting him to the end. He sings with the Psalmist, saying: "The LORD is the strength of my life." "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble" (Ps 46:1).

7.10.3.en: * "God is our refuge and strength" (Ps 46:1). There are refuges in which there is no strength; when one flees to them he grows weaker, not stronger. For example: when you flee to someone greater than you in the world, so as to make a powerful friend for yourself, this seems to me a refuge. Yet how unstable this world is, for the man of authority may be broken from day to day, so when you come to such a refuge you fear all the more... Our refuge is not like this; our refuge is strength. When we flee to Him we are steadfast.

7.10.4.en: St. Augustine In that day also they shall come to thee from Assyria, and from the cities of Egypt, and from Egypt even to the river.

7.11.1.en: The prophet gives them the divine promise of return from captivity, when they come from Babylon to the land of promise, and leave Egypt, to which some of them had fled during the captivity to take refuge in it. They return neither in humiliation nor in fear, but set out "from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain"; that is, without turning back, they go from strength to strength.

7.12.0.en: Notwithstanding the land shall be desolate because of them that dwell therein, for the fruit of their doings. [13]

7.12.1.en: Once again he warns them against returning to sin and corruption after their return from captivity, for God, who gives them strength and honor by returning from captivity to the land of promise, permits the desolation of the land when they return to their old corruption.

7.12.2.en: He calls on God to look upon His flock and His heritage, for it dwells as in rugged places on Mount Carmel; or like sheep lost in a forest, needing a heavenly Shepherd able, with the rod of His tender love, to bring it back to Himself.

7.12.3.en: He asks Him to shepherd them and protect them with His rod and not with the rod of the enemies, for they are His people, and there is none who cares for them as He does! He brings them back from among the forests and rugged mountains to the plains of Bashan and Gilead; He is the great Shepherd of the sheep (Heb 13:20), who lays down His life for them.

7.13.s.en: 3. A final plea on their behalf:

7.13.0.en: 14 Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage, which dwell solitarily in the wood, in the midst of Carmel: let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old. 15 According to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt will I shew unto him marvellous things. 16 The nations shall see and be confounded at all their might: they shall lay their hand upon their mouth, their ears shall be deaf. 17 They shall lick the dust like a serpent, they shall move out of their holes like worms of the earth: they shall be afraid of the LORD our God, and shall fear because of thee.

7.13.1.en: Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage, which dwell solitarily in the wood, in the midst of Carmel.

7.13.2.en: Let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old. [14]

7.13.3.en: Since the prophet realizes that taking refuge in God is prayer, he lifts his heart to God, the good Shepherd, to lead His people with His mercies as in the past, in the glorious days.

7.13.4.en: The prophet calls the people "the flock of God's heritage," for they are the sheep of His pasture (Ps 79:13; 100:3), and His little flock (Lk 12:32), and they are His portion (Jer 12:10), and His inheritance (Ps 94:5), the lot of His inheritance (Deut 32:9). It is as though he asks God to look upon His people, as the Shepherd who cares for His flock, and the Owner who keeps His possession.

7.13.5.en: * "We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture" (Ps 100:3)... This flock is one flock! See what a loving Shepherd we have! He left the ninety and nine and came down to seek the one. He brought it back on His shoulders (Lk 15:4-5), and redeemed it with His blood. This Shepherd died without fear for the flock, He who by His resurrection brought His flock back to Himself.

7.14.0.en: St. Augustine According to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt will I shew unto him marvellous things. [15]

7.14.1.en: God answers the prophet's request and his intercession for his people, and God performs wonders as He did at the exodus from Egypt, when terror fell upon the pagan nations.

7.14.2.en: * Hear what is more wonderful still, that the mysteries of the Old Books, hidden and veiled until now to some extent, are proclaimed by the ancient prophets. For the prophet Micah spoke thus: "According to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt will I shew unto him marvellous things" (Mic 7:15)... Our sins are swallowed up and extinguished in Baptism, just as the Egyptians were drowned in the sea. "He retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy... thou wilt cast all our sins into the depths of the sea" (see Mic 7:19).

7.14.3.en: St. Augustine The nations shall see and be confounded at all their might.

7.15.0.en: They shall lay their hand upon their mouth, their ears shall be deaf. [16]

7.15.1.en: What does the wonderful Shepherd do? He works a wonder with His people. The nations surrounding His people, who gloated over them and stood against them in the day of their calamity, hunting the fugitives and selling them as slaves or handing them over to captivity, now look on. These nations stand astounded before God's care for His people, and they lay their hands upon their mouths and stop their ears, for they cannot utter a single word against the people of God, nor bear to hear their joyful news.

7.15.2.en: This is God's surpassing work with His Church, when she returns to Him in repentance, and with every repentant soul, whom God brings back from disgrace and shame to surpassing inward glories.

7.15.3.en: They shall lick the dust like a serpent, they shall move out of their holes like worms of the earth.

7.16.0.en: They shall be afraid of the LORD our God, and shall fear because of thee. [17]

7.16.1.en: If the nations that resist the divine truth are likened to the creeping things of the earth that lick the dust, then God in His love permits the enemy of good to tempt us, but in the temptation the enemy of good (the ancient serpent) touches only the dust in us, so that we may be proved before God. As St. Ambrose says in his discourse on repentance, the Apostle Paul asked the Corinthians to deliver the fornicator to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit might be saved (1 Cor 5:5), where Satan licks the dust in him, but his soul he does not touch!

7.16.2.en: All that the enemy of good and his hosts can do is to lick the dust that clings to our feet. As the Psalmist says: "and his enemies shall lick the dust" (Ps 72:9). And the Lord Himself says to the Church: "They shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me" (Isa 49:23).

7.16.3.en: Origen says that after his fall sentence was passed upon man: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19), but when he has enjoyed fellowship with the second Adam he hears the divine voice: "You are heaven, and to heaven you shall return." For the work of the good Shepherd is to transform us from the first curse in the first Adam to the blessing in the second Adam, so that we become a holy heaven. Thus the serpent finds nothing in us to eat, since it does not find dust as its food.

7.17.s.en: 4. Magdalah: the victory of divine grace:

7.17.0.en: 18 Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage! He retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy. 19 He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. 20 Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, and the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old.

7.17.1.en: The prophet closes the book with glory to Him, praising God, than whom none is like:

7.17.2.en: a. He is the God of forgiving love [18].

7.18.0.en: b. The God of saving power [19].

7.19.0.en: c. The God of enduring faithfulness [20].

7.19.1.en: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage!

7.19.2.en: He retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy. [18]

7.19.3.en: This is God's delight, to forgive, giving His mercy, declaring His love.

7.19.4.en: Micah uses his name, which means "Who is like God?", to praise God as the forgiver of sins. The wise Solomon sees that the believer who is prudent or wise imitates God, who forgives the transgressions of His brethren who have wronged Him: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Prov 19:11).

7.19.5.en: In his discourse on the equality and unity of the Son and the Father, Pope Athanasius presents this statement about the role of the Father in the forgiveness of sins and then continues: [But the Son said to whom He willed: "Thy sins be forgiven thee." For example, when the Jews murmured, He declared the forgiveness of sins by deed, saying to the paralytic: "Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house" (Mt 9:6)].

7.19.6.en: * "Who can forgive sins but God only?" (Mk 2:7). For since they themselves laid down this definition, they set the rule and proclaimed the law, and He wanted to confound them with their own words. He says: "You have confessed that the forgiveness of sins belongs to God alone, so my equality with Him (the Father) is not open to question." For it is not these men alone who declared this, but the prophet said thus: "Who is a God like unto thee?" and then pointed to His own mark, adding: "that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression" (Mic 7:18). Therefore if someone appears who does the same thing, he is God, the one God. Let us note how Christ conversed with them with meekness and gentleness and all tenderness.

7.19.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * If the Word were a creature, how could He annul God's sentence and forgive sin, when it is written in the prophets that this is the work of God? For "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression?" While God says: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19), and all mankind becomes mortal, how is it within the power of creatures to annul sin? But the Lord Himself annuls it, saying of Himself: "If the Son therefore shall make you free" (see Jn 8:36), so the Son who frees shows truly that He is not a creature nor among creatures, but is the Word by nature, and the image of the Father's essence, who at the beginning issued the sentence (of Adam's death) and who alone blots out sins. And since it was said by the Word: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return," so it became fitting that by the Word Himself and through Him freedom is accomplished and the condemnation is annulled.

7.19.8.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * So that you may know how great is the miracle of the forgiveness of sins, I present to you a prophet as a witness for me. This prophet shows that the forgiveness of sins is the work of no one but God alone when he says: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by sins?" (Mic 7:18). For bringing souls into the Kingdom is greater than destroying death. He led souls into the Kingdom, and He did this by His own power.

7.19.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * Let us not listen to Satan when we are snared in the troubles of the world, whether through bodily pain or the loss of children, or other troubles. Let us not listen to the adversary when he says: "Now, where is the LORD thy God?" (Mic 7:10); when we suffer violent pain we must beware of his temptations, for he tries to lead astray the anxious soul. When the soul looks at the wonderful works of God, it sees itself already in heaven, while Satan crawls around it like a serpent on the earth. Thus the prophet says: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of thine heritage."

7.19.10.en: St. Ambrose He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. [19]

7.19.11.en: God casts our sins into the depths of the sea of His forgiving love, and no longer remembers them. The prophet Jeremiah says: "They are new every morning" (Lam 3:23); so with every morning we look to Him as a Father who forgives the sins of His children, and pours love into their hearts, bringing them always back to Himself. He casts our sins as into the Red Sea with Pharaoh and his hosts, and no longer remembers them. And as it was said of the repentant man: "None of his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live" (Ezek 18:22). And the Lord says: "I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and, as a cloud, thy sins: return unto me; for I have redeemed thee" (Isa 44:22).

7.19.12.en: * It is fitting for us to give a garment to him who has no garment at all. Who is the person without a garment? He is the one who altogether lacks God. Therefore we ought to strip ourselves and give to him who is naked. One has God, and another has no God at all; let us give to him who has no God. The prophet says in Scripture: "We must cast our sins into the sea." John continues: "he that hath meat, let him do likewise" (Lk 3:11). Whoever has food, let him give to him who has none at all. It is fitting for him to give him generously, not only clothing, but also what he can eat.

7.19.13.en: Origen * It is the grace of Baptism to which the prophecy of Micah points: "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins (our sins) into the depths of the sea" (Mic 7:19).

7.19.14.en: St. Jerome Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, and the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old. [20]

7.19.15.en: He is faithful; He promised Abraham mercy beforehand and confirmed His promise to Jacob, and He continues to fulfill His promises to our holy fathers as long as we walk in the spirit of faith working by love.

7.19.16.en: The Lord has sworn, and we believe that He will surely fulfill His promises to us (Heb 6:18-20).

7.19.17.en: O the riches of Your marvelous grace!

7.19.18.en: * You loved me, Your beloved vineyard!

7.19.19.en: You gave me every possibility to establish Your paradise within me!

7.19.20.en: But in foolishness I rejected all Your gifts.

7.19.21.en: I became a barren wilderness without fruit!

7.19.22.en: I turned into a land that brings forth thorns and thistles!

7.19.23.en: * My hands turned to the work of evil.

7.19.24.en: And my mind was occupied with what is not fitting to You.

7.19.25.en: And my heart was too narrow for love.

7.19.26.en: The prince, the judge, and the great man within me were corrupted.

7.19.27.en: I became a brier and a thorn, of no use!

7.19.28.en: * I lost my inner peace, so that I no longer trust a friend, nor confide in a companion or a relative!

7.19.29.en: My depths turned into a battlefield.

7.19.30.en: A struggle between the desires of the flesh and the desires of the Spirit!

7.19.31.en: And strife between reason and emotion.

7.19.32.en: Everything within me fell into great confusion!

7.19.33.en: * Your voice called me and raised me from humiliation.

7.19.34.en: You lifted me from slavery to the glorious liberty of the children of God.

7.19.35.en: Now I cry out in the face of the ancient serpent, saying:

7.19.36.en: Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me!

7.19.37.en: * Your discipline of me has turned into honor and glory!

7.19.38.en: You brought me out of the pit of sin into the paradise of Your righteousness!

7.19.39.en: You set me free to pass from strength to strength, and to rise on the wings of Your Holy Spirit from glory to glory!

7.19.40.en: How wonderful is Your shepherding, O good Shepherd!

7.19.41.en: * In all my afflictions the serpent was not able to bite me, but licked all the dust that clung to my feet, and You made me a new heaven in which Your righteousness dwells!

7.19.42.en: You gave me victory upon victory by Your marvelous grace!

7.19.43.en: * Glory to You, who pardon iniquity and pass by transgression!

7.19.44.en: Glory to You, who are full of mercy and compassion!
